title: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Sexual Selection”. Scope: animals with male-male competition for mates, especially mammals and birds

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a conventional comparative hypothesis with a clear predicted association. Existing compilations can test mammals, birds and some other groups, but not animals generally.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across a phylogenetically controlled sample, regress observed male combat intensity and weapon presence or size on mating-system polygyny. Higher combat and weapon prevalence in polygynous species support the claim; no association or stronger effects in monogamous species refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trait databases have substantial missingness and study bias.

Combat intensity and 'special weapons' require subjective coding.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.83
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.69
data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mating system and weapon presence are standard comparative variables with an obvious phylogenetic contrast, and the trees needed to run it are public. The trait columns themselves still have to be compiled, especially for combat frequency, so the work is months of harmonization rather than a download. Within mammals the test would be informative, with the usual confound that horns and large males are not used only for fighting.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Code mating system, male-combat frequency, and presence of weapons, then fit a phylogenetic regression. The claim would be confirmed if polygynous lineages have higher combat rates and weapon frequencies than monogamous relatives after body size and habitat are controlled; it would be refuted if weapon evolution is independent of mating system. Combat itself is usually proxied by weaponry and sexual size dimorphism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Weapons proxy fighting and can also function in display or predator defence.

Mating system and weapon inventories are spread through handbooks and supplements rather than one global table.

Birds are less consistently coded than large mammals.

operationalizability: 0.76
